title: Python Beginner
description: Variables, data types, conditionals, loops and lists — the foundations of Python programming.

theory.contentHtml:
Python is a high-level programming language created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991. Today, Python is one of the most popular languages in the world - especially in Data Science, Machine Learning, and automation.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Why learn Python?
  2. Your first program: print()
  3. Strings and quotes
  4. Special characters (Escape Characters)
  5. Comment - Notes in code
  6. Printing multiple values with print()
  7. Important Notes

Why learn Python?

  • Simple, readable syntax: Python reads almost like natural English, very friendly to beginners.
  • Versatile: web (Django, Flask), data analysis (Pandas, NumPy), AI/ML (TensorFlow, PyTorch), automation.
  • Huge community: millions of developers and open-source libraries to support you.
  • No compilation needed: run line by line and see the result immediately.

Your first program: print()

By programming tradition, the first program always prints "Hello, World!":

print("Hello, World!")

Just a single line! Compare that with Java, which needs at least 5 lines to do the same thing. The print() function is the most basic tool - used to display information on the screen.

You can print several lines in a row:

print("Hello, Vietnam!")
print("I am learning Python")
print("Year 2024")

Result:

Hello, Vietnam!
I am learning Python
Year 2024

Strings and quotes

Text in Python must be placed inside quotes - you can use single quotes ' or double quotes ", both are valid:

print('Single quotes work fine')
print("Double quotes work too")
print("It's a beautiful day")   # String contains ' → use ""
print('He said "hello"')        # String contains " → use ''

When a string contains a quote inside it, use the other quote type on the outside - to avoid confusion.

Special characters (Escape Characters)

Sometimes you need to print characters that cannot be typed directly - use the \ (backslash) in combination:

+-----------+--------------+-------------------+
| Character |    Meaning   |      Example      |
+-----------+--------------+-------------------+
| \n        | New line     | "Line 1\nLine 2"  |
| \t        | Tab (indent) | "Name:\tAlex"     |
| \\        | Backslash    | "C:\\Users\\Alex" |
| \'        | Single quote | 'It\'s OK'        |
| \"        | Double quote | "He said \"OK\""  |
+-----------+--------------+-------------------+
print("Full name:\tAlex Drew")
print("Address:\n123 Main Street\nNew York")
print("Path: C:\\Users\\Alex\\Desktop")

Result:

Full name:	Alex Drew
Address:
123 Main Street
New York
Path: C:\Users\Alex\Desktop

Comment - Notes in code

Comments are Python lines that are not executed - used to explain the meaning of the code to the reader (or to your future self):

# This is a single-line comment - Python ignores it completely
print("Hello")  # A comment can also follow a statement

# Use comments to temporarily disable code while debugging:
# print("This line will not run")
print("This line still runs normally")

Multi-line comments use triple quotes:

"""
This is a multi-line comment.
Often used to describe what
a complex block of code does.
"""
print("The program still runs normally")

Printing multiple values with print()

The print() function can print several values at once, separated by commas:

print("Name:", "Alex", "- Age:", 25)
print(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
print("Result:", 10 + 20)

Result:

Name: Alex - Age: 25
1 2 3 4 5
Result: 30

By default, print() separates values with a space and adds a newline after each call. You can change this behavior:

print("A", "B", "C", sep="-")    # A-B-C (separated by -)
print("Hello", end=" ")          # No newline at the end
print("there!")                  # Hello there!

Important Notes

  • print() in Python 3 requires parentheses - writing print "Hello" causes a SyntaxError.
  • A string must open and close with the same quote type - 'Hello" is an error.
  • Comments make code easier to read, but don't overuse them - good code explains itself.
  • Use \n when you want a line break inside a string instead of calling print() multiple times.

Before writing any program, you need to master Python's basic syntax rules. These are the "traffic laws" that every Python programmer must follow.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Indentation - The most important rule
  2. Why does indentation matter?
  3. The colon (:) - Required before a code block
  4. Naming Conventions
  5. Case Sensitivity
  6. Reserved Keywords
  7. Writing multiple statements on one line
  8. Line breaks in long expressions
  9. Important Notes

Indentation - The most important rule

In C, Java, or JavaScript, you use curly braces {} to group statements into blocks. In Python, indentation is the syntax - it decides which statement belongs to which block:

if True:
    print("This line is inside the if block")
    print("This line is also inside the if block")
print("This line is OUTSIDE the if block - no indent")

The PEP 8 standard (Python's official style guide): use 4 spaces for each indentation level. Do not use Tabs.

Why does indentation matter?

Indentation is not just "for looks" - it completely changes the program's logic:

score = 8

# Case 1: both lines belong to the if block
if score >= 5:
    print("You passed!")
    print("Congratulations!")   # Only printed when score >= 5

# Case 2: the second line is OUTSIDE the if block
if score >= 5:
    print("You passed!")
print("Congratulations!")       # Always printed, whatever the score

The two snippets above differ by just a few spaces but produce completely different results!

The colon (:) - Required before a code block

Every statement that opens a block (if, for, while, def, class) must end with a ::

# Correct
if True:
    print("OK")

for i in range(3):
    print(i)

# Wrong - missing the colon
if True
    print("Error")   # SyntaxError: expected ':'

Naming Conventions

Python uses snake_case for variables and functions - lowercase, with words separated by an underscore _:

# Variables: snake_case
score_avg = 8.5
student_full_name = "Alex Smith"
product_quantity = 100

# Constants: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE
MAX_SCORE = 10
PI = 3.14159
DAYS_PER_WEEK = 7

# Class names: PascalCase (covered in the advanced course)
class Student:
    pass

Case Sensitivity

Python is case-sensitive - name, Name, NAME are three completely different variables:

name = "Alex"
Name = "Brian"
NAME = "David"

print(name)   # Alex
print(Name)   # Brian
print(NAME)   # David

Reserved Keywords

Python has 35 keywords that you cannot use as variable names:

False   None    True    and     as      assert
async   await   break   class   continue def
del     elif    else    except  finally  for
from    global  if      import  in      is
lambda  nonlocal not     or      pass    raise
return  try     while   with    yield
# Wrong - using keywords as variable names
if = 5           # SyntaxError
for = "loop"     # SyntaxError
class = "12A1"   # SyntaxError

# Correct - use other meaningful names
condition = 5
loop_type = "for loop"
class_name = "12A1"

Writing multiple statements on one line

Python allows writing multiple statements on the same line, separated by ; - but this is not recommended because it's hard to read:

# Valid but not recommended
x = 1; y = 2; z = 3

# Better written separately
x = 1
y = 2
z = 3

Line breaks in long expressions

When an expression is too long, use \ or parentheses () to break the line:

# Way 1: backslash
total = 100 + 200 + \
        300 + 400

# Way 2: parentheses (recommended)
total = (100 + 200 +
         300 + 400)

print(total)   # 1000

Important Notes

  • Always use 4 spaces for indentation - do not use Tabs, do not mix Tabs and Spaces.
  • Do not forget the : after if, for, while, def, class.
  • Name variables in snake_case and give them clear meaning.
  • Python is case-sensitive - name differs from Name differs from NAME.
  • Do not use reserved keywords as variable names.

theory.contentHtml:
A variable is a name given to a memory location used to store data. Think of a variable as a label stuck on a box - you put data into the box, stick a label on it, and whenever you need the data you just call the label's name.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Assigning values to variables
  2. Variable naming rules
  3. Dynamic Typing - Flexible data types
  4. The type() function - Checking data types
  5. The len() function - String length
  6. None - The "nothing" value
  7. f-string - Embedding variables in strings
  8. Real-world example: Student information
  9. Important Notes

Assigning values to variables

Use the = sign to assign a value to a variable. Python automatically determines the data type - you don't need to declare the type like in C or Java:

student_name = "Alex Drew"
age = 25
score_avg = 8.5
graduated = True

Important: The = sign in Python is assignment, not an equality comparison. The equality comparison uses ==.

Variable naming rules

# VALID
name = "Alex"
_private_var = 10         # Starting with _ is also fine
math_score_2024 = 9       # Contains digits but doesn't start with one
item_count = 50           # snake_case - the Python convention

# INVALID
2score = 8             # Starts with a digit → SyntaxError
full name = "Alex"     # Contains a space → SyntaxError
for = 10               # Reserved keyword → SyntaxError

Dynamic Typing - Flexible data types

Python is a dynamically typed language - a variable can freely change its data type during execution:

x = 10        # x is currently an int
print(x)      # 10

x = "hello"   # Now x is a str - perfectly valid
print(x)      # hello

x = 3.14      # Now x is a float
print(x)      # 3.14

The type() function - Checking data types

Use type() to see what data type a variable currently holds:

name = "Brian"
age = 22
score = 8.5
passed = True
empty_value = None

print(type(name))         # <class 'str'>
print(type(age))          # <class 'int'>
print(type(score))        # <class 'float'>
print(type(passed))       # <class 'bool'>
print(type(empty_value))  # <class 'NoneType'>

The len() function - String length

len() returns the number of characters in a string (including whitespace):

name = "Alex Drew"
print(len(name))   # 9

empty_string = ""
print(len(empty_string))   # 0

None - The "nothing" value

None is a special value in Python, meaning "no data" or "not yet assigned":

result = None
print(result)        # None
print(type(result))  # <class 'NoneType'>

# Check for None with is (not ==)
if result is None:
    print("No result yet")

f-string - Embedding variables in strings

An f-string (formatted string) is the most concise way to combine variables and text when printing:

name = "Alex"
age = 25
score_avg = 8.567

# The old way (verbose)
print("Name: " + name + ", Age: " + str(age))

# f-string (preferred)
print(f"Name: {name}, Age: {age}")
print(f"Average score: {score_avg:.2f}")  # Rounded to 2 decimals: 8.57

# You can compute directly inside {}
print(f"Birth year: {2024 - age}")   # 1999

Reading :.2f piece by piece

The part after : inside the braces is called a format specifier. It tells Python how to turn a value into a string for display.

In {amount:,.2f}:

+------+-------------------------------------------+
| Part |                  Meaning                  |
+------+-------------------------------------------+
| :    | Starts the formatting rules               |
| ,    | Adds commas as thousands separators       |
| .2   | Displays 2 digits after the decimal point |
| f    | Displays the number in fixed-point form   |
+------+-------------------------------------------+
amount = 1234567.891

print(f"{amount:.2f}")
print(f"{amount:,.2f}")
print(amount)

Output:

1234567.89
1,234,567.89
1234567.891

:.2f rounds the displayed string to 2 decimal places. It does not change the value stored in amount, so the final print(amount) still prints the original value.

Real-world example: Student information

full_name = "Brian Cooper"
student_id = "SV2024001"
math_score = 8
physics_score = 7.5
chemistry_score = 9

total_score = math_score + physics_score + chemistry_score
avg_score = total_score / 3

print(f"Student: {full_name}")
print(f"Student ID: {student_id}")
print(f"Average score: {avg_score:.2f}")
print(f"Data type: {type(avg_score)}")

Result:

Student: Brian Cooper
Student ID: SV2024001
Average score: 8.17
Data type: <class 'float'>

Important Notes

  • Give variables meaningful names: math_score instead of x, customer_name instead of s.
  • Use f-strings instead of concatenating strings with + - it's both concise and easier to read.
  • None is different from 0, different from "", different from False - each has its own meaning.
  • Using a variable that hasn't been assigned raises a NameError.
  • Use type() and len() frequently when debugging to inspect your data.

theory.contentHtml:
Now that you know how to create basic variables, this lesson introduces more advanced assignment techniques - assigning multiple variables at once, swapping values, and deleting variables.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Assigning multiple variables at once (Multiple Assignment)
  2. Assigning the same value to multiple variables
  3. Swapping values (Swap)
  4. Swapping multiple variables
  5. Deleting variables with del
  6. Real-world example: Managing information
  7. Unpacking from a list or tuple
  8. Checking whether a variable exists
  9. Important Notes

Assigning multiple variables at once (Multiple Assignment)

Python lets you assign values to multiple variables on the same line:

# Assign each variable a value
name, age, score = "Alex", 25, 8.5
print(name)    # Alex
print(age)   # 25
print(score)   # 8.5

The number of variables on the left must exactly match the number of values on the right, otherwise it errors:

# Wrong - 2 variables but 3 values
a, b = 1, 2, 3   # ValueError: too many values to unpack

# Wrong - 3 variables but 2 values
a, b, c = 1, 2   # ValueError: not enough values to unpack

Assigning the same value to multiple variables

When several variables need the same initial value:

x = y = z = 0
print(x, y, z)   # 0 0 0

# Application: initialize counters
correct_count = wrong_count = skipped_count = 0

Swapping values (Swap)

In most other languages, swapping the values of two variables needs a temporary variable. Python has an especially concise way:

a = 10
b = 20

# The usual way (needs a temp variable)
temp = a
a = b
b = temp
print(a, b)   # 20 10

# The Python way (concise and fast)
a = 10
b = 20
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)   # 20 10

How it works: Python evaluates the entire right-hand side (b, a) first, then assigns to the left-hand side (a, b).

Swapping multiple variables

This technique works with any number of variables:

a, b, c = 1, 2, 3
a, b, c = c, a, b    # Rotate
print(a, b, c)       # 3 1 2

Deleting variables with del

Use del to delete a variable - freeing memory and preventing accidental use:

tmp_name = "temporary value"
print(tmp_name)   # temporary value

del tmp_name
# print(tmp_name)   # NameError: name 'tmp_name' is not defined

del is useful when you want to make sure a variable no longer exists after you are done with it:

# Delete multiple variables at once
x = 1
y = 2
z = 3
del x, y, z

Real-world example: Managing information

# Initialize student info
first_name, middle_name, last_name = "Alex", "James", "Smith"
full_name = f"{first_name} {middle_name} {last_name}"
print(f"Full name: {full_name}")

# Swap shift assignments
morning_shift = "Alex"
afternoon_shift = "Brian"
print(f"Before: Morning={morning_shift}, Afternoon={afternoon_shift}")

morning_shift, afternoon_shift = afternoon_shift, morning_shift
print(f"After: Morning={morning_shift}, Afternoon={afternoon_shift}")

Result:

Full name: Alex James Smith
Before: Morning=Alex, Afternoon=Brian
After: Morning=Brian, Afternoon=Alex

Unpacking from a list or tuple

The multiple-assignment technique also applies to lists and tuples:

# Unpacking list
coords = [10.5, 20.3]
x, y = coords
print(f"x={x}, y={y}")   # x=10.5, y=20.3

# Unpacking tuple
info = ("Alex", 25, "Hanoi")
name, age, city = info
print(f"{name}, {age} years old, in {city}")

Checking whether a variable exists

Sometimes you need to check whether a variable has been created before using it:

# Use try/except to check
try:
    print(undefined_var)
except NameError:
    print("The variable does not exist!")

Important Notes

  • When assigning multiple variables, the number of variables must match the number of values - otherwise you get a ValueError.
  • a, b = b, a is the standard swap in Python - concise, fast, and Pythonic.
  • del deletes a variable permanently - reusing it causes a NameError.
  • Don't overuse multiple assignment on one line if it makes the code hard to read.
  • Unpacking is very useful when working with data returned from a function or from a list.

practice.summaryHtml:
Platform practices run several inputs, so a solution belongs in a function instead of hard-coding the sample data.

Define and call a function

1def add_tax(price, rate):
2 result = price * (1 + rate)
3 return result
4
5print(add_tax(100, 0.1))

  • def starts the definition; names in parentheses are parameters.
  • The function body must share one indentation level.
  • return sends a value back to the caller and ends that call.
  • print only displays text; it does not replace return when the task asks for a returned value.

Every branch still needs a result

1def grade_label(score):
2 if score >= 8:
3 return "excellent"
4 if score >= 5:
5 return "pass"
6 return "retry"
7
8print(grade_label(7))

Read a practice prompt as three parts: function name, parameters, and the value to return. Tests call the function with several inputs; hard-coded sample output passes only one case.

questions.prompt: Which function is used to print information to the screen in Python?
questions.explanation: print() is a built-in Python function used to display information on the screen. In Python 3, parentheses are required.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

name = 'Alex'
print(f'Hello, {name}!')
questions.explanation: An f-string (with an f before the quote) lets you embed variables directly into a string using the {variable_name} syntax. The result is Hello, Alex!.

questions.prompt: Which variable name follows the Python standard (PEP 8)?
questions.explanation: Following the PEP 8 standard, Python uses snake_case for variables and functions - lowercase, separated by _. UPPER_SNAKE_CASE is for constants, and PascalCase is for classes.

questions.prompt:
What does the following code print?

a, b = 10, 20
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)
questions.explanation: a, b = b, a is the value-swapping syntax in Python. Python evaluates the entire right-hand side (b=20, a=10) first, then assigns to the left-hand side. Result: a=20, b=10.

questions.prompt: What does type(3.14) return?
questions.explanation: 3.14 is a real number (it has a decimal part), so Python classifies it as float. An integer like 3 is int.

theory.contentHtml:
Python has two main numeric types: integers (int) and floating-point numbers (float). Understanding these two types is the foundation for doing any calculation in Python.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. int - Integers
  2. float - Floating-point numbers
  3. Arithmetic operators
  4. Operator precedence
  5. Compound assignment operators
  6. Numeric type conversion
  7. round() - Rounding numbers
  8. Other useful numeric functions
  9. Important Notes

int - Integers

int stores whole numbers (no decimal part). Notably, Python does not limit the size of integers - you can compute with extremely large numbers without worrying about overflow:

age = 25
score = -3
population = 98_000_000   # The _ makes numbers easier to read
huge_number = 10 ** 100   # Python handles it!

print(type(age))   # <class 'int'>
print(population)       # 98000000

float - Floating-point numbers

float stores real numbers (with a decimal part):

score_avg = 8.5
pi = 3.14159
temperature = -2.7
ratio = 0.75          # 75%

print(type(score_avg))   # <class 'float'>

Arithmetic operators

+----------+-----------------------------------+---------+--------+
| Operator |              Meaning              | Example | Result |
+----------+-----------------------------------+---------+--------+
| +        | Addition                          | 7 + 3   | 10     |
| -        | Subtraction                       | 7 - 3   | 4      |
| *        | Multiplication                    | 7 * 3   | 21     |
| /        | Division (always yields float)    | 7 / 2   | 3.5    |
| //       | Floor division (integer quotient) | 7 // 2  | 3      |
| %        | Modulo (remainder)                | 7 % 2   | 1      |
| **       | Exponentiation                    | 2 ** 8  | 256    |
+----------+-----------------------------------+---------+--------+
# Real-world example: computing salary
base_salary = 10_000_000
coefficient = 1.5
bonus = 2_000_000

net_salary = base_salary * coefficient + bonus
print(f"Salary: {net_salary:,.0f} VND")
# Salary: 17,000,000 VND

Operator precedence

Python follows mathematical rules: exponentiation > multiplication/division > addition/subtraction. Use parentheses () to change the order:

print(2 + 3 * 4)      # 14 (multiplication first)
print((2 + 3) * 4)    # 20 (parentheses first)
print(10 - 3 + 2)     # 9  (left to right)
print(2 ** 3 ** 2)    # 512 (exponentiation: right to left)

Compound assignment operators

score = 10
score += 2    # score = score + 2 → 12
score -= 3    # score = score - 3 → 9
score *= 2    # score = score * 2 → 18
score /= 3    # score = score / 3 → 6.0
score //= 2   # score = score // 2 → 3.0
print(score)  # 3.0

Numeric type conversion

int() converts to an integer (truncating the decimal part, not rounding). float() converts to a real number:

# int() - truncates the decimal part
print(int(3.9))      # 3  (no rounding!)
print(int(3.1))      # 3
print(int("42"))     # 42 (converts a numeric string)

# float() - converts to a float
print(float(5))        # 5.0
print(float("3.14"))   # 3.14

round() - Rounding numbers

print(round(3.14159, 2))   # 3.14
print(round(3.7))           # 4
print(round(2.5))           # 2  (banker's rounding)
print(round(3.5))           # 4

# Application: computing an average score
avg_score = (8 + 7 + 9.5) / 3
print(round(avg_score, 2))   # 8.17

Other useful numeric functions

# abs() - absolute value
print(abs(-15))     # 15
print(abs(3.7))     # 3.7

# min() / max() - smallest / largest
print(min(5, 3, 8, 1))   # 1
print(max(5, 3, 8, 1))   # 8

# divmod() - quotient and remainder at once
quotient, remainder = divmod(17, 5)
print(f"17 / 5 = {quotient} remainder {remainder}")   # 17 / 5 = 3 remainder 2

Important Notes

  • The / division always returns a float, even 10 / 2 gives 5.0 - use // if you want an int.
  • int("3.14") raises a ValueError - you must use int(float("3.14")).
  • % (modulo) is very useful: checking even numbers (x % 2 == 0), splitting hours/minutes/seconds.
  • round(2.5) gives 2 (not 3) due to banker's rounding - rounding to the nearest even number.
  • Use _ in large numbers for readability: 1_000_000 instead of 1000000.

A string is a data type used to store text - customer names, addresses, product descriptions, emails. When working with real data, you will use str a lot.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Creating strings
  2. Concatenating (+) and repeating (*) strings
  3. Indexing - Accessing each character
  4. Slicing - Extracting substrings
  5. len() - String length
  6. Common string methods
  7. Searching and replacing
  8. split() and join() - Splitting/Joining strings
  9. Strings are immutable
  10. Important Notes

Creating strings

A string is enclosed in single quotes ' or double quotes ". Multi-line strings use triple quotes """ or ''':

s1 = 'Single quotes'
s2 = "Double quotes"
s3 = """A string
spanning multiple lines
uses triple quotes"""

print(s1)   # Single quotes
print(s3)
# A string
# spanning multiple lines
# uses triple quotes

Concatenating (+) and repeating (*) strings

first_name = "Alex"
last_name = "Drew"
full_name = first_name + " " + last_name
print(full_name)   # Alex Drew

divider = "-" * 30
print(divider)   # ------------------------------

Indexing - Accessing each character

Each character in a string has an index, starting from 0:

s = "Python"
#    P  y  t  h  o  n
#    0  1  2  3  4  5   (index from the left)
#   -6 -5 -4 -3 -2 -1   (index from the right)

print(s[0])    # P  - first character
print(s[-1])   # n  - last character
print(s[2])    # t

Slicing - Extracting substrings

Syntax: s[start:stop:step] - take from start up to (but not including) stop, stepping by step:

s = "Python"
print(s[0:3])    # Pyt  (from 0 up to 3)
print(s[2:])     # thon (from 2 to the end)
print(s[:4])     # Pyth (from the start up to 4)
print(s[::2])    # Pto  (step 2)
print(s[::-1])   # nohtyP (reversed)

Practical application:

employee_id = "EMP_2024_001"
year = employee_id[4:8]
print(year)   # 2024

len() - String length

name = "Alex Drew"
print(len(name))   # 9 (spaces are counted)

empty_string = ""
print(len(empty_string))   # 0

Common string methods

Python provides dozens of built-in methods for strings:

name = "  emma jane WATSON  "

# Upper/lower case
print(name.upper())      # "  EMMA JANE WATSON  "
print(name.lower())      # "  emma jane watson  "
print(name.title())      # "  Emma Jane Watson  "

# Remove surrounding whitespace
print(name.strip())      # "emma jane WATSON"
print(name.lstrip())     # "emma jane WATSON  "
print(name.rstrip())     # "  emma jane WATSON"

Searching and replacing

address = "123 Main Street, District 1, New York"

# find() - position of the first occurrence (-1 if not found)
print(address.find("District"))   # 17
print(address.find("London"))     # -1

# count() - count occurrences
print(address.count(","))   # 2

# replace() - substitute text
new_address = address.replace("New York", "Boston")
print(new_address)   # 123 Main Street, District 1, Boston

# in - membership check
print("District" in address)   # True

split() and join() - Splitting/Joining strings

# split() - split a string into a list
text = "London, Paris, Tokyo"
cities = text.split(", ")
print(cities)   # ['London', 'Paris', 'Tokyo']

# join() - join a list into a string
result = " | ".join(cities)
print(result)   # London | Paris | Tokyo

Strings are immutable

Strings in Python cannot be changed character by character - you must create a new string:

s = "hello"
# s[0] = "H"   # TypeError!
s = "H" + s[1:]   # Create a new string: "Hello"
print(s)   # Hello

Important Notes

  • Indexing starts at 0, not 1 - s[0] is the first character.
  • String methods return a new string, they do not modify the original - you must reassign: s = s.upper().
  • s[::-1] is the fastest way to reverse a string.
  • "word" in s is simpler than s.find("word") != -1.
  • When chaining methods: s.strip().lower().replace(" ", "_") - runs left to right.

A boolean is a data type with exactly two values: True and False. It is the foundation of every conditional statement, loop, and piece of logic in a program.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. True and False
  2. Comparison operators
  3. Logical operators: and, or, not
  4. Truthy and Falsy
  5. Chained Comparison
  6. Precedence of logical operators
  7. Important Notes

True and False

The two boolean values are capitalized - True and False (not true/false as in JavaScript):

is_logged_in = True
in_stock = False

print(type(is_logged_in))   # <class 'bool'>

# Bool is a subclass of int: True = 1, False = 0
print(True + True)    # 2
print(True * 5)       # 5
print(False + 1)      # 1

Comparison operators

A comparison operator takes two values and returns True or False:

+----------+-----------------------+---------------+
| Operator |        Meaning        |    Example    |
+----------+-----------------------+---------------+
| ==       | Equal                 | 5 == 5 → True |
| !=       | Not equal             | 5 != 3 → True |
| >        | Greater than          | 5 > 3 → True  |
| <        | Less than             | 5 < 3 → False |
| >=       | Greater than or equal | 5 >= 5 → True |
| <=       | Less than or equal    | 3 <= 5 → True |
+----------+-----------------------+---------------+
score = 8.5
print(score >= 5)       # True  (passed)
print(score == 10)      # False (not a perfect score)
print(score != 5)       # True  (not equal to 5)

# Compare strings (alphabetical/Unicode order)
print("abc" < "abd")          # True
print("Python" == "python")   # False (case-sensitive)

Logical operators: and, or, not

Used to combine multiple conditions:

age = 20
has_id = True

# and - both must be True
is_eligible = age >= 18 and has_id
print(is_eligible)   # True

# or - at least one condition is True
free_ticket = age < 6 or age > 60
print(free_ticket)   # False

# not - negation
under_age = not (age >= 18)
print(under_age)   # False

Combining multiple real-world conditions:

exam_score = 8
conduct_score = 7

# Excellent student: both scores >= 8
excellent_student = exam_score >= 8 and conduct_score >= 8
print(f"Excellent student: {excellent_student}")   # False (conduct is only 7)

# Gets an award: at least one score >= 9
gets_award = exam_score >= 9 or conduct_score >= 9
print(f"Gets an award: {gets_award}")   # False

Truthy and Falsy

In Python, many values can be used as booleans in a condition. The falsy values (treated as False):

print(bool(0))       # False - the number 0
print(bool(0.0))     # False - float zero
print(bool(""))      # False - empty string
print(bool([]))      # False - empty list
print(bool(None))    # False - the None value

Every other value is truthy (treated as True):

print(bool(1))       # True
print(bool(-1))      # True - non-zero number
print(bool("abc"))   # True - non-empty string
print(bool([1, 2]))  # True - list with elements

Application - a cleaner way to check for an empty string or empty list:

name = ""
if not name:
    print("Name must not be empty")

items = [1, 2, 3]
if items:
    print(f"There are {len(items)} elements")

Chained Comparison

Python lets you write chained comparisons just like in math:

score = 7.5

# Pythonic - concise and readable
if 5 <= score < 7:
    print("Average")
elif 7 <= score < 9:
    print("Good")

# Equivalent full version
if score >= 5 and score < 7:
    print("Average")

Precedence of logical operators

Order: not > and > or. Use parentheses () for clarity:

# Without parentheses - easy to misread
print(True or False and False)    # True (and runs first)

# With parentheses - clear
print((True or False) and False)  # False
print(True or (False and False))  # True

Important Notes

  • Confusing = (assignment) with == (comparison) is a very common mistake - if x = 5: is a SyntaxError.
  • Check for None with is instead of ==: if x is None: (more Pythonic).
  • not can be applied to any value: not 0 → True, not "hello" → False.
  • Precedence: not > and > or - when in doubt, use parentheses ().
  • True/False are capitalized - true/false cause a NameError.

lessons.title: Branching with if, elif and else
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 15: Branching with if, elif and else

theory.contentHtml:
In life, we constantly make decisions: "If it rains, bring an umbrella; if not, walk". In programming, the if/elif/else statement does exactly that - it lets the program choose an action based on a condition.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Basic if structure
  2. if...else - Two branches
  3. if...elif...else - Multiple branches
  4. Combining multiple conditions
  5. Nested if - nested ifs
  6. Real-world example: Calculating shipping fees
  7. Important Notes

Basic if structure

The simplest syntax - run a statement if the condition is true:

score = 8

if score >= 5:
    print("You passed!")
    print("Congratulations!")

Result: Both lines are printed because 8 >= 5 is True.

Important: The statements belonging to the if block must be indented by 4 spaces. Any line that is not indented lies outside the if block.

if...else - Two branches

When you want to handle both the true and false cases:

age = 16

if age >= 18:
    print("Old enough to vote")
else:
    print("Not old enough to vote")
    print(f"{18 - age} more years to go")

Result:

Not old enough to vote
2 more years to go

if...elif...else - Multiple branches

When there are more than two cases, use elif (short for "else if"):

score = 7.5

if score >= 9:
    grade = "Excellent"
elif score >= 7:
    grade = "Good"
elif score >= 5:
    grade = "Average"
else:
    grade = "Weak"

print(f"Score {score} → Grade: {grade}")

Result: Score 7.5 → Grade: Good

Python checks from top to bottom - when it hits the first true condition it runs that block and skips all the elif/else below.

Combining multiple conditions

Use and, or, not to combine multiple conditions:

age = 25
has_license = True
years_experience = 2

if age >= 18 and has_license and years_experience >= 1:
    print("Eligible to drive")
else:
    print("Not eligible yet")

Nested if - nested ifs

You can place an if inside another if - each level is indented by another 4 spaces:

score = 9
conduct = "Good"

if score >= 8:
    print("Academic level: Excellent")
    if conduct == "Good":
        print("Awarded the Excellent Student title")
    else:
        print("Title not awarded (conduct not good enough)")
else:
    print("Academic level below Excellent")

Result:

Academic level: Excellent
Awarded the Excellent Student title

Real-world example: Calculating shipping fees

order_value = 500_000
area = "suburban"

if order_value >= 1_000_000:
    shipping_fee = 0
    note = "Free shipping"
elif area == "inner-city":
    shipping_fee = 15_000
    note = "Inner-city shipping"
else:
    shipping_fee = 30_000
    note = "Suburban shipping"

total = order_value + shipping_fee
print(f"Order: {order_value:,} VND")
print(f"Shipping fee: {shipping_fee:,} VND ({note})")
print(f"Total: {total:,} VND")

Result:

Order: 500,000 VND
Shipping fee: 30,000 VND (Suburban shipping)
Total: 530,000 VND

Important Notes

  • Don't forget the : after if, elif, else - missing it is a SyntaxError.
  • Indentation must be consistent - 4 spaces per level, don't mix Tabs with Spaces.
  • elif is written as one word, not else if (unlike JavaScript/C).
  • Python checks from top to bottom and stops at the first True - the order of conditions matters.
  • Avoid nesting ifs too deeply (3+ levels) - the code becomes hard to read and maintain, so split it into separate functions or use elif.

After mastering if/elif/else, this lesson introduces techniques for writing conditions more concisely and efficiently - making your Python code more "Pythonic".

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Chained Comparison - Comparison chaining
  2. Ternary Operator - One-line conditional expression
  3. The in Operator - Membership test
  4. Real-world example: BMI classification
  5. Example: Login check
  6. Guard Clause - Check early, exit early
  7. Important Notes

Chained Comparison - Comparison chaining

Python lets you write successive comparisons like a mathematical expression:

score = 7.5

# The usual way
if score >= 5 and score < 7:
    print("Average")

# The Pythonic way - shorter and easier to read
if 5 <= score < 7:
    print("Average")

# You can chain multiple comparisons
x = 5
if 1 < x < 10:
    print(f"{x} is in the range (1, 10)")

if 1 <= x <= 5 <= 10:
    print("Chaining multiple comparisons")

Ternary Operator - One-line conditional expression

When you only need to assign a value based on a simple condition:

age = 20

# The usual way (4 lines)
if age >= 18:
    status = "Adult"
else:
    status = "Minor"

# Ternary (1 line) - syntax: value_if_true if condition else value_if_false
status = "Adult" if age >= 18 else "Minor"
print(status)   # Adult

You can use it directly inside print() or an f-string:

score = 8
print(f"Result: {'Pass' if score >= 5 else 'Fail'}")
# Result: Pass

number = 7
label = "even" if number % 2 == 0 else "odd"
print(f"{number} is {label}")   # 7 is odd

The in Operator - Membership test

in checks whether a value is contained in a collection (list, string, tuple):

# Check in a list
fruits = ["apple", "orange", "mango", "grape"]
if "orange" in fruits:
    print("Orange is in the list")

# Check in a string
email = "alex@xomdata.com"
if "@" in email:
    print("Valid email")

# not in - check that something is NOT there
if "durian" not in fruits:
    print("No durian")

Use it to replace many elif branches:

color = "red"

# Instead of writing many elifs:
# if color == "red" or color == "orange" or color == "yellow":

if color in ["red", "orange", "yellow"]:
    print("Warm color")
elif color in ["blue", "green", "purple"]:
    print("Cool color")
else:
    print("Other color")

Real-world example: BMI classification

weight = 65   # kg
height = 1.70   # m

bmi = weight / (height ** 2)

if bmi < 18.5:
    category = "Underweight"
elif 18.5 <= bmi < 25:
    category = "Normal"
elif 25 <= bmi < 30:
    category = "Overweight"
else:
    category = "Obese"

print(f"BMI: {bmi:.1f} → {category}")

Result: BMI: 22.5 → Normal

Example: Login check

username = "admin"
password = "xomdata123"

if not username or not password:
    print("Please fill in all fields")
elif username == "admin" and password == "xomdata123":
    print("Login successful!")
else:
    print("Wrong username or password")

Guard Clause - Check early, exit early

Instead of deeply nested ifs, check the failing condition and exit early:

# Deeply nested (hard to read)
def process_order(price, quantity):
    if price > 0:
        if quantity > 0:
            total = price * quantity
            print(f"Total: {total}")
        else:
            print("Quantity must be > 0")
    else:
        print("Price must be > 0")

# Guard clause (easier to read)
def process_order_v2(price, quantity):
    if price <= 0:
        print("Price must be > 0")
        return
    if quantity <= 0:
        print("Quantity must be > 0")
        return
    total = price * quantity
    print(f"Total: {total}")

Important Notes

  • Use ternary only for simple conditions - if complex, use a full if/else for readability.
  • in is very useful when checking a value against many options - instead of writing many ors.
  • Chained comparison a <= x < b only works in Python - other languages don't support it.
  • Avoid overly deep nested ifs - use elif or a guard clause to keep code flat and readable.
  • not in is the official syntax - written as one, not not (x in list).

theory.contentHtml:
A list is the most important data structure when you start learning Python. A list holds multiple values in a single variable, and the for loop lets you go through each element.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Creating a List
  2. Indexing - Accessing elements
  3. The for loop - Iterating over each element
  4. range() - Creating a sequence of numbers
  5. Combining for, range, and list
  6. enumerate() - Getting index and value together
  7. Practical example: Finding the highest score
  8. Important Notes

Creating a List

A list is created with square brackets [], with elements separated by commas:

# List of numbers
scores = [8, 7.5, 9, 6, 8.5]

# List of strings
student_names = ["Alex", "Brian", "David", "Emma"]

# Mixed list (rarely used)
mixed = ["Alex", 25, True, 8.5]

# Empty list
empty_list = []

print(scores)       # [8, 7.5, 9, 6, 8.5]
print(len(scores))  # 5

Indexing - Accessing elements

Like strings, indexing starts at 0:

fruits = ["apple", "orange", "mango", "grape", "melon"]
#            0         1        2        3        4
#           -5        -4       -3       -2       -1

print(fruits[0])    # apple  (first element)
print(fruits[-1])   # melon  (last element)
print(fruits[2])    # mango

# Change a value (lists are mutable!)
fruits[1] = "pomelo"
print(fruits)   # ['apple', 'pomelo', 'mango', 'grape', 'melon']

The for loop - Iterating over each element

for iterates over each element in a list (or any iterable):

student_names = ["Alex", "Brian", "David"]

for name in student_names:
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

Result:

Hello, Alex!
Hello, Brian!
Hello, David!

Iterate over a list of numbers and compute the sum:

scores = [8, 7, 9, 6, 8]
total = 0

for s in scores:
    total += s

print(f"Total: {total}")                    # 38
print(f"Average: {total / len(scores)}")    # 7.6

range() - Creating a sequence of numbers

range() produces a sequential range of numbers - very often used with for:

# range(stop) - from 0 to stop-1
for i in range(5):
    print(i, end=" ")   # 0 1 2 3 4
print()

# range(start, stop) - from start to stop-1
for i in range(2, 6):
    print(i, end=" ")   # 2 3 4 5
print()

# range(start, stop, step) - with a step
for i in range(0, 10, 2):
    print(i, end=" ")   # 0 2 4 6 8
print()

# Count down
for i in range(5, 0, -1):
    print(i, end=" ")   # 5 4 3 2 1

Combining for, range, and list

names = ["Alex", "Brian", "David", "Emma"]

# Iterate with an index
for i in range(len(names)):
    print(f"{i + 1}. {names[i]}")

Result:

1. Alex
2. Brian
3. David
4. Emma

enumerate() - Getting index and value together

subjects = ["Math", "Physics", "Chemistry", "English"]

for idx, subject in enumerate(subjects, start=1):
    print(f"{idx}. {subject}")

Result:

1. Math
2. Physics
3. Chemistry
4. English

Practical example: Finding the highest score

scores = [7, 9, 5, 8, 10, 6]
highest_score = scores[0]

for s in scores:
    if s > highest_score:
        highest_score = s

print(f"Highest score: {highest_score}")   # 10

Important Notes

  • Indexing starts at 0 - the first element is my_list[0], not my_list[1].
  • Lists are mutable - unlike strings (immutable).
  • range(5) produces the sequence 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 - it does not include 5.
  • Use enumerate() instead of range(len()) when you need both the index and the value.
  • for automatically stops when there are no more elements - no need to check a stop condition like with while.

lessons.title: Conditional loops with while, break, continue
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 21: Conditional loops with while, break, continue

theory.contentHtml:
While for is used when you know the number of iterations in advance, while is used when you don't know in advance - it loops until a condition becomes False. Python also provides break, continue, pass to control the loop flow.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. The while loop
  2. while vs for - When to use which?
  3. break - Exit the loop immediately
  4. continue - Skip the current iteration
  5. pass - Do nothing (placeholder)
  6. while + break - A loop with an exit condition
  7. Practical example: Summing up to a threshold
  8. for + else / while + else
  9. Important Notes

The while loop

while checks the condition before each iteration - if True it runs, if False it stops:

counter = 1

while counter <= 5:
    print(f"Round {counter}")
    counter += 1   # Important: you must update the condition variable!

print("Done")

Result:

Round 1
Round 2
Round 3
Round 4
Round 5
Done

Warning: If you forget counter += 1, the loop will run forever without stopping (infinite loop)!

while vs for - When to use which?

# for - the number of iterations is known in advance
for i in range(5):
    print(i)

# while - unknown in advance, depends on a condition
num = 1000
while num > 1:
    num = num // 2
    print(num, end=" ")   # 500 250 125 62 31 15 7 3 1

break - Exit the loop immediately

break stops the loop entirely and jumps out:

# Find the first even number in the list
numbers = [3, 7, 5, 4, 9, 2]

for num in numbers:
    if num % 2 == 0:
        print(f"First even number: {num}")
        break

Result: First even number: 4 - it does not continue to 9 and 2.

continue - Skip the current iteration

continue skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next one:

# Print odd numbers from 1 to 10 (skip evens)
for i in range(1, 11):
    if i % 2 == 0:
        continue   # Skip even numbers, jump back to the top of the loop
    print(i, end=" ")   # 1 3 5 7 9

pass - Do nothing (placeholder)

pass is an "empty" statement - Python requires every block to have at least one line, and pass is used when you haven't written the logic yet:

for i in range(10):
    if i % 2 == 0:
        pass   # TODO: handle even numbers later
    else:
        print(f"{i} is odd")

while + break - A loop with an exit condition

# Guess the number: loop until the guess is correct
secret_number = 7
attempts = 0

while True:   # Infinite loop
    attempts += 1
    guess = attempts * 2 + 1   # Simulated guess
    if guess == secret_number:
        print(f"Correct! Guessed in {attempts} attempts.")
        break
    if attempts > 10:
        print("Out of attempts!")
        break

Practical example: Summing up to a threshold

# Keep adding 1+2+3+... until the total >= 100
total = 0
n = 0

while total < 100:
    n += 1
    total += n

print(f"We need to add up to {n} for the total to reach >= 100")
print(f"Total = {total}")

Result:

We need to add up to 14 for the total to reach >= 100
Total = 105

for + else / while + else

Python has a special syntax: else after a loop - it runs when the loop finishes normally (not interrupted by break):

# Check whether a number is prime
num = 17

for i in range(2, num):
    if num % i == 0:
        print(f"{num} is not a prime number")
        break
else:
    print(f"{num} is a prime number")

Result: 17 is a prime number

Important Notes

  • while must have a way to stop - if the condition is always True and there is no break, the program runs forever.
  • break exits the entire loop, continue only skips the current iteration.
  • pass is just a placeholder - used when you need to keep the code structure but have no logic yet.
  • Use for when you know the number of iterations, while when it depends on a condition.
  • while True: ... break is a common pattern for loops waiting for input or an event.

lessons.title: Working with lists using append, sort and pop
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 22: Working with lists using append, sort and pop

theory.contentHtml:
In the previous lesson you learned to create a list and iterate over it with for. This lesson introduces the methods for adding, removing, sorting, and searching for elements in a list.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Adding elements
  2. Removing elements
  3. Sorting
  4. Reversing
  5. Searching and counting
  6. len(), sum(), min(), max()
  7. Practical example: Managing a student list
  8. Important Notes

Adding elements

fruits = ["apple", "orange"]

# append() - add to the end
fruits.append("mango")
print(fruits)   # ['apple', 'orange', 'mango']

# insert(index, value) - insert at a given position
fruits.insert(1, "grape")
print(fruits)   # ['apple', 'grape', 'orange', 'mango']

# extend() - append another list
fruits.extend(["melon", "pear"])
print(fruits)   # ['apple', 'grape', 'orange', 'mango', 'melon', 'pear']

Note: append(["a", "b"]) adds the whole sublist, whereas extend(["a", "b"]) adds each element individually.

Removing elements

items = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]

# remove(value) - remove an element by value (first occurrence)
items.remove("c")
print(items)   # ['a', 'b', 'd', 'e']

# pop(index) - remove by index and return the removed value
element = items.pop(1)   # Remove index 1
print(element)   # b
print(items)        # ['a', 'd', 'e']

# pop() - no index → remove the last element
last = items.pop()
print(last)   # e
print(items)     # ['a', 'd']

# del - remove by index (does not return the value)
del items[0]
print(items)   # ['d']

Sorting

numbers = [5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3]

# sort() - sorts the list in place (modifies the original)
numbers.sort()
print(numbers)   # [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9]

# sort(reverse=True) - sort in descending order
numbers.sort(reverse=True)
print(numbers)   # [9, 8, 5, 3, 2, 1]

# sorted() - returns a new list, the original is unchanged
numbers2 = [5, 2, 8]
numbers2_sorted = sorted(numbers2)
print(numbers2)          # [5, 2, 8] (unchanged)
print(numbers2_sorted)   # [2, 5, 8]

Reversing

items = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

# reverse() - reverses in place
items.reverse()
print(items)   # [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]

# Or use slicing (does not change the original)
items2 = [1, 2, 3]
print(items2[::-1])   # [3, 2, 1]
print(items2)         # [1, 2, 3] (unchanged)

Searching and counting

scores = [8, 7, 9, 8, 6, 8]

# index(value) - position of the first occurrence
print(scores.index(9))   # 2

# count(value) - count the occurrences
print(scores.count(8))   # 3

# in - check existence
print(9 in scores)    # True
print(10 in scores)   # False

len(), sum(), min(), max()

numbers = [4, 7, 2, 9, 1]

print(len(numbers))    # 5 - number of elements
print(sum(numbers))    # 23 - sum
print(min(numbers))    # 1 - smallest
print(max(numbers))    # 9 - largest

# Compute the average
avg = sum(numbers) / len(numbers)
print(f"Average: {avg}")   # 4.6

Practical example: Managing a student list

students = []

# Add students
students.append("David")
students.append("Alex")
students.append("Emma")
students.append("Brian")
print(f"There are {len(students)} students: {students}")

# Remove a student who dropped out
students.remove("David")
print(f"After removal: {students}")

# Sort by name
students.sort()
print(f"Sorted: {students}")

Result:

There are 4 students: ['David', 'Alex', 'Emma', 'Brian']
After removal: ['Alex', 'Emma', 'Brian']
Sorted: ['Alex', 'Brian', 'Emma']

Important Notes

  • sort() and reverse() modify the original list in place and return None - do not assign the result.
  • sorted() returns a new list - the original is unchanged.
  • remove() only removes the first occurrence - if the value is not found it raises ValueError.
  • pop() returns the removed value - useful when you need the element you just removed.
  • The in operator is very fast for existence checks: if "Alex" in students.

theory.contentHtml:
input() pauses a program and always returns a string. In this course's sandbox, practices receive data through function parameters so tests can run automatically; the input() examples below are marked norun.

Read and convert a value

name = input("Enter your name: ").strip()
age_text = input("Enter your age: ").strip()

if age_text.isdigit():
    age = int(age_text)
    print(f"Hello {name}, age {age}")
else:
    print("Age must be a non-negative integer")

isdigit() is suitable for this simple non-negative-integer example. Negative numbers, decimals, and detailed error handling need try/except, which Python Intermediate teaches; do not call int() before validation when errors are not handled.

Read several values

split() separates the string into parts. Use the loop you already know to convert each part, without a list comprehension:

parts = input("Enter non-negative integers: ").split()
numbers = []
valid = True
for part in parts:
    if part.isdigit():
        numbers.append(int(part))
    else:
        valid = False

if valid:
    print(sum(numbers))
else:
    print("Invalid input")

Key points

  • input() always returns str; convert only after validation.
  • strip() removes outer whitespace and split() separates fields.
  • Sandbox practices use function parameters rather than waiting for a keyboard.
  • try/except and list comprehensions belong to the next course; this lesson does not require them early.

This is the final lesson of the Python Basics course - a summary of everything you've learned: variables, data types, operators, branching, loops, and lists. Each example combines several concepts to solve a real-world problem.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Example 1: Managing class scores
  2. Example 2: Filtering data from a list
  3. Example 3: Writing an aggregate function
  4. Example 4: String processing + conditions
  5. Example 5: Loops + accumulation
  6. Important Notes

Example 1: Managing class scores

Combines: list, for, if/elif, f-string, computation functions.

class_scores = [8, 6.5, 9, 4, 7, 3.5, 8.5, 5, 10, 6]

# Classify
excellent = 0
good = 0
average = 0
weak = 0

for s in class_scores:
    if s >= 8:
        excellent += 1
    elif s >= 6.5:
        good += 1
    elif s >= 5:
        average += 1
    else:
        weak += 1

print(f"Class size: {len(class_scores)}")
print(f"Excellent: {excellent}, Good: {good}, Average: {average}, Weak: {weak}")
print(f"Class average: {round(sum(class_scores) / len(class_scores), 2)}")
print(f"Highest: {max(class_scores)}, Lowest: {min(class_scores)}")

Result:

Class size: 10
Excellent: 4, Good: 2, Average: 2, Weak: 2
Class average: 6.75
Highest: 10, Lowest: 3.5

Example 2: Filtering data from a list

Combines: list, for, if, append, f-string.

data = [15, -3, 0, 22, -8, 7, -1, 30, 0, 12]

positives = []
negatives = []
zero_count = 0

for num in data:
    if num > 0:
        positives.append(num)
    elif num < 0:
        negatives.append(num)
    else:
        zero_count += 1

print(f"Positive ({len(positives)}): {positives}")
print(f"Negative ({len(negatives)}): {negatives}")
print(f"Zeros: {zero_count}")

Result:

Positive (5): [15, 22, 7, 30, 12]
Negative (3): [-3, -8, -1]
Zeros: 2

Preview: this example briefly introduces a dictionary and .items() so you can recognize a labelled result. Both are taught fully in Python Intermediate and are not required by this course's practices.

Example 3: Writing an aggregate function

Combines: def, for, if, list methods, return dict.

def analyze_list(nums):
    """Analyze a list of numbers."""
    if len(nums) == 0:
        return {"count": 0}

    total = 0
    maximum = nums[0]
    minimum = nums[0]

    for num in nums:
        total += num
        if num > maximum:
            maximum = num
        if num < minimum:
            minimum = num

    average = round(total / len(nums), 2)

    return {
        "count": len(nums),
        "total": total,
        "average": average,
        "maximum": maximum,
        "minimum": minimum
    }

# Usage
result = analyze_list([4, 8, 2, 10, 6])
for key, value in result.items():
    print(f"{key}: {value}")

Result:

count: 5
total: 30
average: 6.0
maximum: 10
minimum: 2

Example 4: String processing + conditions

Combines: str methods, for, if, list.

email_list = [
    "  Alex@Gmail.COM  ",
    "invalid-email",
    "  brian@xomdata.com",
    "",
    "david@YAHOO.com  "
]

valid_emails = []
invalid_emails = []

for email in email_list:
    email_clean = email.strip().lower()
    if "@" in email_clean and "." in email_clean:
        valid_emails.append(email_clean)
    else:
        invalid_emails.append(email_clean if email_clean else "(empty)")

print(f"Valid ({len(valid_emails)}):")
for e in valid_emails:
    print(f"  - {e}")

print(f"Invalid ({len(invalid_emails)}):")
for e in invalid_emails:
    print(f"  - {e}")

Example 5: Loops + accumulation

# Compute the factorial n! = 1 * 2 * 3 * ... * n
def factorial(n):
    result = 1
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        result *= i
    return result

for n in range(1, 8):
    print(f"{n}! = {factorial(n)}")

Result:

1! = 1
2! = 2
3! = 6
4! = 24
5! = 120
6! = 720
7! = 5040

Important Notes

  • When writing a complex program, break it into steps - handle each part then combine them.
  • Use functions (def) to reuse code and keep the program tidy.
  • Always handle edge cases: empty list, zero, empty string.
  • Name variables clearly - highest_score is better than x, valid_emails is better than nums.
  • Use round() when printing floats to avoid long results like 6.666666666667.
  • The next course, Intermediate Python, will teach: dictionary, tuple, set, advanced functions, file I/O, list comprehension.
